notes.urn:cts:latinLit:tmp1057.tmp1057.opp-lat: Editorial bracketed variants and comments in the printed text (e.g. on the omission of 'in', 'dicant', 'Bonifacius', the alternative 'secundo loco ... bona') have been left out. 'in lide' read as 'in fide' (in faith); a manuscript variant 'in fine' (to the end) is noted by the edition. 'ut mihi est' rendered following Harduin's correction 'vae mihi est'. The name of the second candidate for Larissa is lost in the text ('et... presbytero'). 'Misericordiam consecutus sum' is cited by the edition as I Cor. VII. The letter quoted at the end of ab4/4 is not given in this stretch; the text seems to break before 'gestaque confecit'. 'Of which faith is the head': the edition prints 'quorum canat est ludes', which makes no sense; the translation follows 'quorum caput est fides', which the damaged letters fit.

Line 4: 'apud de- fensorem civitatis' taken as the civic official, the defensor civitatis. 'Si qua est... dilectio transite' is difficult; 'transite' (cross over) may be corrupt. 'Brevis' read as an inventory. In the second petition 'nec... demissum' read as 'permissum' (allowed); 'relicta fuisset sententia' read as 'relecta' (read out); 'observaturum esse' taken as 'I would remain'. The citation 'I Cor. VI' is in fact 2 Cor. 6:2.

Line 10: 'Thebanæ' refers to Phthiotic Thebes in Thessaly. 'Dicæsariensis' taken as Diocaesarea; 'Laminensis' as Lamia. Line 14: 'liberatum' is evidently a scanning error, read as 'librorum' (books); possibly 'litterarum' (letters).

nodes.text: THE LETTERS AND DECREES OF POPE BONIFACE II.
FIRST LETTER (FORMERLY ELEVENTH).
POPE BONIFACE II TO CAESARIUS OF ARLES.
At his request he confirms what had been defined at the Synod of Orange.
To his most beloved brother Caesarius, Boniface.

Through our son Armenius, priest and abbot, we have received the letter of your fraternity, which, as it seems, you had sent to us while still unaware of the priestly office entrusted to me, in that charity by which we are bound in God; in it you had thought it right to ask that what you had requested of our predecessor of blessed memory, Pope Felix, for the strengthening of the catholic faith, should be carried through by my urging. But since the will on high has so disposed that what you had hoped to obtain from him through us you should rather obtain from us, we have not delayed to give a catholic reply to your petition, which you conceived out of praiseworthy concern. For you report that some bishops of the Gauls, while they now agree that the other goods come from the grace of God, would have faith alone, by which we believe in Christ, to be of nature, not of grace; and that it has remained in the free will of men from Adam, which it is wicked to say, and is not also now conferred on individuals by the bounty of divine mercy. You ask that, to remove the ambiguity, we should confirm by the authority of the apostolic see your confession, in which you, on the contrary, define, in accordance with catholic truth, that right faith in Christ and the beginning of all good will is inspired in the minds of individuals by the prevenient grace of God. And so, since many Fathers, and above the rest Bishop Augustine of blessed memory, and also our forebears the prelates of the apostolic see, are shown to have discussed this matter so very fully and with reason that it ought to be doubtful to no one any longer that faith itself also comes to us from grace, we have thought it right to refrain from a lengthy reply; above all since, according to those sentences which you have cited from the Apostle, where he says: 'I have obtained mercy, so that I might be faithful' (I Cor. VII); and elsewhere: 'To you it has been given for Christ's sake, not only that you believe in him, but also that you suffer for him' (Philip. I), it plainly appears that the faith by which we believe in Christ, like all good things, comes to individual men from the gift of grace on high, not from the power of human nature. We rejoice that your fraternity too, having held a conference with certain bishops of the Gauls, has judged this in accordance with the catholic faith: namely in those points in which, as you have reported, they defined with one consent that the faith by which we believe in Christ is conferred by the prevenient grace of the Godhead; rejecting also [the idea that there is] anything at all good according to God which anyone can either will, or begin, or perform, or complete without the grace of God, since our Saviour himself says: 'Without me you can do nothing.' For it is certain and catholic that in all good things, of which faith is the head, divine mercy goes before us while we are still unwilling, so that we may will; is present in us when we will; and follows also so that we may endure in faith; as the prophet David says: 'My God, his mercy shall go before me' (Psal. LVIII); and again: 'My mercy is with him' (Psal. LXXXVIII); and elsewhere: 'His mercy shall follow me' (Psal. XXII). Likewise blessed Paul says: 'Or who has first given to him, and it shall be repaid to him? For from him and through him and in him are all things' (Rom. XI). Hence we greatly wonder at those who think otherwise, that they are still so weighed down by the remnants of the ancient error as to believe that one comes to Christ not by the gift of God but by nature; and that they say the good of nature itself, which is known to have been corrupted by Adam's sin, is the author of our faith rather than Christ; and do not understand that they are protesting against the Lord's sentence, which says: 'No one comes to me unless it has been given to him by my Father' (John VI); and are at the same time also opposing blessed Paul, who cries out to the Hebrews: 'Let us run to the contest set before us, looking to Jesus Christ, the author and finisher of faith' (Hebr. XII). This being so, we cannot find what they attribute to the human will, without the grace of God, for believing in Christ, since Christ is the author and finisher of faith. Therefore, greeting you with fitting affection, we approve your confession written above as consonant with the catholic rules of the Fathers. As for those who, as you report, would attribute the other [goods] to grace while faith comes first, we bind them by their own profession, so that they are compelled far rather to ascribe faith too to the gift of grace, without which there is nothing good that anyone can do according to God, as the blessed Apostle says: 'Everything that is not of faith is sin' (Rom. XIV). This being so, either they will attribute no good to grace, if they strive to withdraw faith from it; or if they say that any good is from grace, faith itself must necessarily be attributed to grace. For if there is nothing good without faith, and yet faith itself is denied to come from grace, then no good, God forbid, will have to be attributed to grace. For the apostle James says: 'Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights' (Jac. I). And they themselves admit, as you say, that the other gifts are given through grace; and they do not doubt that all goods themselves subsist through faith. Faith itself, therefore, must necessarily be attributed to grace, since they cannot separate from it the good which they attribute to grace. These points having thus been briefly set out, we have not thought it necessary to reply to the remaining absurdities of the Pelagian error which that letter seems to contain, which you reported was sent to you by a certain bishop: for we hope from the divine mercy that through the ministry and teaching of your fraternity he will deign so to work in the hearts of all whom you reported as dissenting, that from this they may believe that all good will proceeds not from themselves but from divine grace, when they find that they now wish to defend what they were stubbornly striving to attack. For it is written: 'The will is prepared by the Lord' (Prov. XIX, according to the LXX), and elsewhere: 'I know that I cannot be continent unless God gives [it], and this itself was [a mark] of wisdom, to know whose gift this was' (Wis. VIII). May God keep you safe, dearest brother. Given on the eighth day before the Kalends of February, in the consulship of Lampadius and Orestes, men of senatorial rank (A.D. 530).
THREE PETITIONS OF STEPHEN TO BONIFACE. FIRST PETITION.
To my lord, holy and in all things most blessed, and truly venerable father of fathers, universal patriarch Boniface, Stephen, a lowly bishop.

Not relying on unreasonable confidence, nor ignorant of my own mediocrity, but with a contrite soul and a humble spirit, and with many tears, I offer you this my supplication, and I therefore think it acceptable before you, most blessed father: for formerly also those who supplicated God with tears prayed with confidence, as if with burnt offerings and rams and bulls, and indeed with ten thousand fat lambs: for 'God will not despise a contrite and humbled heart' (Psal. L). So neither will you, most holy father, hold me in contempt, surrounded as I am by many evils and looking only to God and, by paternal custom, to your piety. Since no ecclesiastical order can surpass that power of yours which was conferred on you by the Saviour of all and first shepherd, nothing is small or lowly to which your providence looks. The more you surpass all before God, the more you must reflect that this is the proof of those who love God, as Peter, after God the father and leader of the holy Church, testifies to you and to the whole world. For when the Lord said for the third time: 'Do you love me? Feed my sheep' (John XXI), he handed over the commands, showing [them] first to you, and then through you bestowed them on all the holy Churches throughout the whole world. Finally, it is for this reason that those who were made venerable before you, all who were found worthy to hold that holy see, while living in body in the glorious city of Rome, yet in spirit adorned all that was duly done and passed beyond [it]; and very many members of the body of the Church have been set free from the violence of slandering enemies by God and the venerable apostolic see. Hence I beseech you: judge the humble, and do justice to the poor, as it is written (Psal. LXXXI). For in secular life I formerly held a provincial rank in the service, and I passed my life humbly and modestly, as it was. But when Proclus of blessed memory, who had been made bishop of the Church of Larissa, went to his rest, and a prelate had to be ordained for that Church, a decree was made jointly by the clergy as well as the people, the metropolitan, and those whose assent was necessary for the act; and, according to ancient custom, three were chosen: Alexander, a priest of Sciathos, and ..., a priest, and my lowly self; and having obtained the better testimony I won the palm of election. But I, knowing myself, judged myself unworthy of so great a task; yet I gladly assented to it all by the grace and clemency of God, looking to the thief and the publican and very many other examples of this kind, whom God suddenly snatched from extreme evils and, as one must say, from the very depth of evils; by these I was encouraged, and a certain hope of a good purpose was given me. So all of them conferred the election on me in God, subscribing together to the decree. And since according to ancient custom the ordination had to take place not elsewhere but in the same city, the holy synod of the province assembled, together with the landowners of the whole city and the whole body of the Church, and with the common testimony of all, nothing departing from custom, I was ordained bishop in the church. For Probianus, beloved of God, bishop of the city of Demetrias, showed such eagerness in this matter, and so embraced what had been done, that he even took it upon himself to deliver praise in the Church of God on the person of my humble self. And so that, without my saying anything about myself, it may be understood from those who wanted and elected me that this ordination came about according to God. Therefore I beseech you, most blessed father, to deign to hear these things gently; for I do not put them forward out of love for the praise of my own lips, as it is written, since he who glories in himself cannot be approved before God, but so that, once you know these things, the calumny raised against me may plainly appear to you. How much the bishops of the province and the clergy of the holy Church then said, showing that they rejoiced at my election, I have judged superfluous for your ears. So while the enemy of all good things was quiet, and God did not look upon my sins, the Church suffered no disturbance, and the charity of all was covering offences, as it is written. But, incited from I know not where, Antonius, a God-fearing priest and steward, and Probianus the defamer, bishop of the city of Demetrias (I mean, most blessed one, that same Probianus who, pushing aside others hastening to speak my praises, himself delivered in the church before God the titles of my praise), persuading Demetrius, beloved of God, bishop of the city of Sciathos, and others alike to be partners in their faction, not ashamed of the subscriptions contained in the decree, nor Probianus of his own praise and the testimony of the whole Church, nor of what they had said or done, how they embraced my ordination, how my person had been pleasing to them even before the ordination, how they gladly accepted the ordination once performed, suddenly set out for the imperial city, and, composing a certain accusation, laid complaints before the most holy archbishop of that same city, Epiphanius, saying that my ordination did not at all accord with the holy canons, hoping that another bishop might be substituted in my place. As I begin to speak of these things, distress certainly holds me back. For if I tell what they have done against me, or the storm that now hangs over my life, or the things they threaten, since they are fiercer, [I fear] that someone may judge me insolent or bold for saying anything about the prelate of so great and so important a Church. But if I keep silent about them, woe is me; for where do I have help? But committing myself to the judgement of our great God and Saviour Jesus Christ, and of your beatitude, and of the piety of the most serene emperor, I could not keep silent. So when the accusation against me had reached the most holy archbishop Epiphanius (again and again I ask pardon for what I am about to say; judge it, most holy fathers, to be not of insolence or boldness but of necessity), he made a *commonitorium* [an instruction], as they call it, addressed to Andrew, a most religious man, deacon and notary of his holy Church, and sent it to the province of Thessaly, ordering me to withdraw from the sacred ministry as not ordained according to the canons; using no proof of the accusations nor canonical summons, he suspended the other bishops of the same province and the clergy of our holy Church from communion with me, and, what is the last straw, he did not even allow me to have food or necessities from the property of the Church: rather, what is usually done to the convicted he is known to have done to me before any examination of judgement took place. Indeed, for those who truly offend, very many mercies have been established by the Churches. These things, then, Andrew, the religious man I mentioned above, was ordered to carry out against me. And so that he might produce me in person to answer to the judgement of him who had suspended me from communion, he was ordered at the same time to produce Eustathius, bishop of the city of Gomphi, and Elpidius of Thebes, and also Stephen of Lamia, as if they were the instigators of my unlawful ordination. But Demetrius and Probianus, religious men, who had earlier been a great part of my election and ordination, he who was driving me to trial kept with him and supported wholly for my ruin. But the aforesaid religious man Andrew did not find me there, since I had set out a little before for the great city of Thessalonica; but having gathered the clergy and as many others as he could find, he read the *commonitorium* to them, and the letter addressed to them. Now the letter written to the clergy by that same most holy man was as follows: and drew up a record before the defender of the city, copies of which I have not failed to append to my humble petitions. An inventory was also made of the sacred vessels and the church's property; and some were removed from the care of church affairs by Antonius, a religious man, who everywhere connived with the religious man Andrew. This aforesaid Andrew, coming to the great city of Thessalonica, showed me, and Elpidius and Stephen, the aforesaid bishops beloved of God, what had been ordered and threatened. But I, fearing the efforts neither of the accusers nor of anyone else, and looking only to God, and to the laws of the holy Church, and to the primacy of the holy Churches entrusted to you, at once said in the record that if I had to answer to any accuser, or if he deigned to judge anything concerning my ordination, it was necessary for me to plead my case, but elsewhere, before one with whom the law of the sacred canons is kept and custom is observed to this day, making mention of your holy head and of the apostolic see; saying that you are the lords of this examination; and begging that nothing new should be done against me, nor anything that could disturb what was well ordered. For what place of remedy would have remained to me with you, most blessed lords of judgement, if I had not said these things? And I did not only say this, but I also showed certain documents that would help the case. These records that were made, which I have attached to my humble petitions, make known both the decree passed against me and the testimonials of praise. I indeed thought that this pledge of my appeal could have served my cause, if, once you to whom it has been given by God to judge had been named, an incompetent person would withdraw. For God is not [a God] of confusion, but of peace (1 Cor. 14:33). Yet neither these nor other things could suffice for my peace; but I was brought against my will to the royal city. And had not certain men who fear God, looking to and awaiting the promise laid up for visiting prisons, promised that I would be present, I would certainly have been put in chains, a man harming no one, as I believe, except that I consented to those who elected me, and, committing myself to hope in God, was found worthy to be ordained; and because I said confidently that if any examination had to take place, it ought to be made by him who has been appointed lord of this examination; and other things which were done to me, and which I do not doubt are being carried out. I am being pressed, and I have no time to breathe; nor shall I be able to find anyone to take thought for me in such great calamities. I confess I am suffering worse things from those who threaten me; condemnation, exile, and whatever penalties for crimes there are, I await undeservedly. Therefore, trusting in you and in your apostolic see, I now ask of you the one remedy: for hope, as the divine word says, will not be put to shame (Rom. 5). And if there were anyone presiding whom the holy canons determined to be judge in this matter, he ought, as I think, first to judge and examine the life of the accusers; because they cannot be accusers of one who, however humble, has been found worthy of the honour of the episcopate. But since, as I said, I have given offence because of my trust in you, these things have been set forth on my side, and I have been placed in the evils I named above; and therefore I beg you, if there is any mercy of God, if any compassion, if any love, cross over, and here likewise, in the Holy Spirit, according to the blessed apostle, bring me help, remembering yourselves and your predecessors of that blessed see, since they never allowed anyone to be unjustly harmed by anyone. If you swiftly succour the oppressed, I trust that I shall be saved from my evils with the same speed; but if, God forbid, my sins delay your compassion, at least if something has been done quickly by those who lie in wait, even so it befits you to stand by the holy canons and to carry out what has been neglected. For this is your work, most blessed one, day and night to guard the laws and statutes of the holy Fathers and of your venerable and apostolic see in all the Churches, but especially in your province of Illyricum. And in another hand: I, Stephen, lowly bishop of the holy Church of Larissa, have signed with my own hand this petition made by me, and have sent it to my lord, most holy and in all things most blessed, and also most venerable father of fathers and universal patriarch Boniface.

Abundantius, bishop of the city of Demetrias, rising from the assembly, said: I could not pass over it, hearing the name of Probianus. This Probianus who is in question is the very man who invaded my Church, and when I was coming to your beatitude with letters of the bishop, seizing on my absence, rashly usurped my place, and according to the holy canons he ought not to be called a bishop: against him I ask your beatitude that the discipline of the apostolic see may come to my aid. Bishop Boniface said: Let both the reading of the petition presented and the statement of our brother and fellow bishop Abundantius be entered in the record; and if there is anything else, we wish to learn it. Theodosius, bishop of the city of Echinus in the province of Thessaly, said through an interpreter: The same most holy Stephen, metropolitan bishop, has also sent another petition to your beatitude through my service; I ask that you order it to be read to your hearing. Bishop Boniface said: Let the petition which he offers be received by the notaries and read. And when it had been received, Menas the notary read [it].
SECOND PETITION.
To my lord, holy and most blessed and truly venerable father of fathers and archbishop and patriarch Boniface, a supplication given by Stephen, a lowly [bishop].

The things that were formerly in expectation, and made me fear and tremble and call upon your holy apostolic see, now that they have seized upon and are constraining my wretched life, compel me all the more to appeal to your beatitude. Behold, the acceptable time; behold, now the day of salvation (2 Cor. 6). Deliver me from my enemies, and rescue me from those who persecute me: for the water has poured round me even to my soul, venerable father, and the uttermost deep has surrounded me: let my life rise up from corruption, as it is written. For if the mercies of God do not come first, I have become a work, such as they wished, of my enemies. I weep and mourn, because now the order of the Church too is endangered. For since, according to the great mercy of him who does not reckon sins to men, I was elected and ordained bishop in the city of Larissa, which is in the province of Thessaly, certain of those who elected me, and often confirmed their election in their writings so that I was judged worthy of the priesthood, seeing that it was my aim to restore the ancient custom in our holy Churches, broke away and accused me before the most blessed prelate of the Church of the holy royal city. He, receiving the accusation, and examining beforehand none of the things that ought to be inquired into concerning an accused bishop, at once separated me from all church ministry, sending one of the religious clergy of his holy Church to the province of Thessaly with letters which they call a *commonitorium*. And though these things accord neither with civil order nor with secular laws, nor does the order of the canons plainly allow this to be done, that punishment should come before judicial examination, the divine Scripture having long since most emphatically proclaimed: Do not accept an empty report; nevertheless, when the most religious man who bore the order had come to Thessalonica and wished to dispute some things with me, I at once said to him: It belongs to the apostolic see, that is, to your beatitude, both to hear and to settle the cases of our province. But the most holy archbishop of the royal city, not resting, ordered me, against the canons, to be produced as well. And when I had come, he held an assembly of the bishops staying there, and I did not delay to plead this again, imploring the apostolic see of your holy and blessed head, and [urging] that the custom which has prevailed in our province until now ought not to be overturned; and I begged that the authority of the apostolic see, which, as it was given by our Lord Jesus Christ and by the sacred canons, so has also been preserved by ancient custom, should not be violated in any respect. But he would not depart from his purpose; rather, taking up the hearing, he had one aim: that he should be seen to be lord and judge in the holy Churches of the province of Thessaly. I, therefore, seeing the surging storm, fled to your holy and most safe harbour, and making a petition I sent these very things, setting them out, to your beatitude, begging you to show me the compassion of God and of the holy Church, which always succours those in danger. But those who lie in wait for my life, perceiving, as I think, that you do not disregard what has been done, but pursue it, as is the custom of your holiness, and defend the order of the holy Churches, made every effort to accomplish their will before any decision of yours should arrive. So, though nothing had been proved against me, and no fault worthy of canonical punishment had been found, they pronounced sentence, and condemning me suspended me from the priestly office: though it is clear that I was not allowed to plead more fully on my side; and that when I asked to show some things that would help my case, it was not permitted. Therefore I begged that sentence should not be pronounced before what had been done was referred to you, most blessed ones, so that the examination of the case might thereafter be reserved to you. This statement incited them all the more against me, as they thought something was being taken away from the rights of the sacred churches of the royal city, because I was seen to have named your apostolic see. For I said that the authority of the apostolic see, which was given by God and our Saviour to the chief of the apostles, surpasses all the privileges of the holy Churches, and in its confession all the Churches of the world find rest. So, when the sentence had been read, I again implored your just hearing, before which no one's dispute can disturb your justice; but the fear of God which is in you itself causes each person's rights to be restored through you. And I think, venerable ones, that they, disregarding what they formerly did against me, will do the same things again a second time; and I suspect that they will not rest at this, but will also vent their enmity on my wretched body, so that when I am dead no accuser can appear. For when the sentence had been read, I was at once handed into custody to the defenders of the sacred Church, beloved of God. But some who fear God, pitying my misery because I was destitute on all sides, took me on their surety, promising a large sum of money for me that I would not leave, but would remain in the royal city; all those who contrived these things against me having this as their chief design, that I might not be able to hasten to the footsteps of your beatitude and, according to God's command, receive some mercy from you. I beseech you therefore, have pity on a humble man of distraught mind; help me through the grace conferred on you by the Lord. For if you have received from the word of God the power to forgive other sins also, as the divine Scripture says, that what you loose on earth is loosed also in heaven (Matt. 16), how much more will you have power over the things that have been done and decreed against me? For to you the poor man is left; you are helper of the orphan (Ps. 9); for I am known to be abandoned by all human hope. And in another hand: I, Stephen, lowly [bishop], have signed this my supplication.

Bishop Boniface said: Let what has been read be entered in the church's records. And he added: Since the greater part of the day has gone, at the next session, if you believe anything else remains, do not delay to make it known.
SECOND SESSION.

After the consulship of Lampadius and Orestes, most distinguished men, on the fifth day before the Ides of December, in the consistory of the blessed apostle Andrew, the venerable man Pope Boniface presiding, together with the bishops Sabinus of the city of Canusium, Abundantius of the city of Demetrias, Carosus of the city of Centumcellae, [and] Felix of the city of Nomentum; there also sitting the priests Sanctulus, Mercurius, Vivulus, Peter, Eventius, Albinus, Ursus, Peter, Epiphanius, Benedict, Servus Dei, Gaudiosus, Peter, Valentinus, Renatus, Florentius, Hilarius, Paul, Bacauda, Innocent, Andrew, Gaudiosus, Philip, Crescentio, Libertinus, Januarius, Sebastian, Cyriacus, Vivulus, Dulcitius, John, Pullio, Andrew, Bonus, Laurence, Seleucus, Rusticus, Caelestinus, Barbarus, Laurence, and Redemptus; the deacons Tribunus, Agapitus, Donatus and Probus also standing by; Tribunus the archdeacon said: Theodosius, bishop of the city of Echinus in the province of Thessaly, is waiting, as you ordered at the previous session: what do you command? Boniface, bishop of the Catholic Church of the city of Rome, said: Let him come in. When he had entered, Bishop Boniface said: Now that he has entered, let him set out what he desires. Theodosius, bishop of the city of Echinus in the province of Thessaly, said through an interpreter: Elpidius, Stephen and Timothy, venerable bishops, my brothers of the province of Thessaly, are known to have sent petitions to be offered through me to your sacred beatitude; command that these too be read to you as I offer them. Bishop Boniface said: Let this paper also be made known by the notary's reading. And when it had been received, Menas the notary read [it].
To our lord, holy and most blessed and truly venerable father of fathers and archbishop, Boniface the patriarch, Elpidius, Stephen and Timothy, lowly bishops.

Your beatitude learned some time ago of the necessities that were pressing upon us; and composing a small petition, most holy father, we made known some while ago, declaring them, the evils we have suffered and the harsher ones we expect; and that those who serve the will and threats of the men contriving these things against us have one aim, that Stephen, beloved of God, should be deprived of his episcopal office. But while he was still speaking, another messenger came announcing worse things. For when the earlier things had been done, the most holy prelate of the Church of the royal city and the holy synod that was with him, hearing [of them], persisting in their former will, snatched from us Stephen, beloved of God, the shepherd of us (or: our shepherd) and of the holy Church of Larissa, which is the metropolitan city of the province of Thessaly; composing a sentence of condemnation as it pleased them, they had added that he was not permitted to go to the province of Thessaly. But the aforesaid man, beloved of God, repeatedly protested during the proceedings to the most holy prelate of the royal city and to the synod that had gathered with him, that they were not permitted to take up this hearing, and still less to decree anything, but that this belonged to the beatitude of the apostolic see. They, however, disregarding his protest, and indeed provoked all the more by it, pronounced a merciless sentence. Him they thought to remove in this way from our holy Church; and they were preparing to make for themselves jurisdiction in our province, so that by this example no one should dare to say anything about the rights of our holy Churches, nor make mention of antiquity or of what they have held until now. For their aim is to bring us wretched men under the ordination and jurisdiction of the Church of the holy royal city. For all these things, mourning day and night, we pour out tears to the Saviour of all, Jesus Christ our God, and hold out our wretched grey hairs, begging that you not allow us to be handed over into their hands. For this reason we appeal both to your beatitude and to the apostolic see; and through it we believe that we hear and adore the thrice-blessed Peter and the first shepherd of the holy Church, Christ our Lord: hoping that you will by no means despise the petition of wretched men, which we have presented with a soul full of tribulation and sorrows; but correcting these things with fitting amendment, coming to the aid of these affairs, that you will deign to give a remedy, for our spirit has failed (Ps. 142), as was said in the Psalms by him who prayed in anguish of soul: so that the man beloved of God, who, striving to guard the right of the apostolic see, is seen to have endured such great dangers, may be restored to his office by apostolic authority, [you] providing for the future that the custom of the holy Churches of our province be in no way overturned. For unless the mercy of God and your help come before us, a third or fourth messenger will come bearing similar news, for their intent does not rest with Stephen, beloved of God, but they will do these things to very many others too, and will not rest before they bring their desires to fulfilment. And in another hand: I, Elpidius, lowly bishop of the holy Church of Thebes, petitioning, [had this signed] through John my priest, since for grief I could not sign with my own hand; he signed at my order. I, Timothy, lowly bishop of the holy Church of Diocaesarea, petitioning, have signed. I, Patricius, lowly priest of the holy Church of God of Lamia, coming to the royal city on behalf of Stephen, my holy bishop, at his order, petitioning, have signed.

Bishop Boniface said: Let what has been read be copied. And he added: If there is anything else, let it be put forward. Theodosius, bishop of the city of Echinus in the province of Thessaly, said through an interpreter: From the reading of the petitions your beatitude has learned what has been done against the holy canons and the ordinance of your predecessors. For it is established that the venerable pontiffs of your see, although throughout the whole world the apostolic see rightly claims for itself the primacy of the Churches, and it alone must be appealed to from everywhere in ecclesiastical cases, nevertheless claimed the Churches of Illyricum specially for their own governance. And the writings of all the preceding pontiffs are known to you; nevertheless I produce copies of certain letters, whose authenticity I now ask to be verified from your archive.

Bishop Boniface said: Let the letters produced be read, and let the authenticity of the writings be sought in the archive of the apostolic see. And when the copies of the books had been received, Menas the notary read [them].
